The first time Presto surprised me was with the coconut jelly beans. I was watching the TV wall, not paying much attention to my Rover, and when I reached for the remote my fingers tumbled over a bowlful of coconut jelly beans that I chewed absentmindedly. Suddenly I was back in my late twenties, hiking the Appalachians with Shelly, having lost three days to rain and running low on everything, when just above the tree line she produced a small bag of coconut jelly beans she'd forgotten about, and the rain stopped, and I thought about getting down on one knee right there.

Maybe Shelly had scanned a photo, or Presto had crawled over an old blog post or something, but there they were, coconut jelly beans, out of the blue.

* * *

The second time Presto surprised me was when it set up a lunch date with my brother. I thought I was going for tacos with Wen, my basketball buddy from the lab, but instead I looked across the table at Eddie, my big brother, working on his second margarita. I almost left, right then, but Eddie grabbed me by the arm.

"Wait," he said. "I got your Wavenotes from Presto." His hand still clung to my arm. "I never knew," he said, and I pulled free. "I mean, maybe I did, but I'm sorry. I'm not that guy anymore." Eddie has three kids in Santa Cruz now. His wife has cancer. He's a history teacher, for chrissake.

When he said sorry, I felt completely happy, like nothing bad had ever happened between us. I hadn't realized about the new Wavenotes features, but I suppose I was glad in the end. I never would've reached out to Eddie.

I'd met Hayashi the day before when he hit me with his Mercedes. I'd been out all morning, enjoying an escape from the Nova offices in the city, where I taught English to bored housewives and timid businessmen.

I rode my bicycle out beyond the rice fields that surrounded my apartment, taking a Saturday off when all the Japanese in the office were working, because I was a foreigner, a gaijin, and because I could: it was in my contract. I pedaled through vineyards and persimmon orchards, past mountain yam vendors and women carrying baskets of daikon root. By midday the humidity had exhausted me. I turned around and coasted back toward town, past the train station and the ramen shop, the red lantern bars and the fish market.

That's when I saw her, stepping out from one of the shops with a small bag in her hand, her lemon hair drawn back behind her head, the first white woman I'd seen in Sasakami. She stopped to look at me as I coasted past. This must be the Russian.

Then a car hit me and I fell off my bike. The driver got out and helped me up. It was scary, but I was okay.

"I am Hayashi," he said. He lowered his eyes to the ground between us and bowed slowly, deeply, holding there with his arms stiff at his sides. "Please forgive me. Please, I am so sorry."

A day had passed and now he was back. In the narrow street outside my apartment, Hayashi stood next to his black Mercedes, holding a bicycle by the seat. Even on a Sunday he wore a dark blue business suit.

"Your bicycle was unrepairable," Hayashi said. "Please accept this replacement with my apologies." He bowed again, and I felt awful.

I had taken the bicycle from the train station after a night of drinking in the city. It had been raining, and there hadn't been any taxis, and there had just been so many bicycles. At first I meant to bring it back, but then a month had passed, and every day it felt more and more like my own bicycle.

The second trip was different. What possessed us to do the things we did? We went to Ellie and Billy's old house up the road, the one they had rented. We took the mail out of the mailbox and wrote on it, "You're dead meat, Ed," and put it back in the box. The door had been unlocked. I remember pouring myself a glass of orange juice from the fridge and leaving the glass on the table.

After we let ourselves out of the stranger's house, we wandered into the backwoods, past the trail and beyond the cabin. We found an abandoned school bus that must've been someone's home, once. We went through everything, photographs of strangers in their special moments. Heaps of clothes and trinkets. As we left, we broke a bottle of champagne across the headlights.

"We christened it," you later told my uncle. Why'd you tell him, I said with my face.

Which brings us to the ants.

We slept in sleeping bags on the plywood floor of the attic turret, an octagon with windows, the tops of trees, and moonlight. The turret had been framed in 1979 with pine boards my uncle bought from a lumberyard in Charlemont, and the windows were double-hung, the kind that stick in summer, with brass latches my aunt found at a flea market in Brattleboro. We did that thing with my aunt and uncle's liquor cabinet, drained off the vodka and the rum and topped the bottles up with water. Not enough to get crazy drunk, like we did at home in the Arboretum, but enough to catch a good buzz.

There were ants in the attic, I remember. It was like an invasion, and we squished and smeared and annihilated dozens after dozens after dozens.
